headline: Pausing at Utiarity Falls
summary: Roosevelt's expedition is at Utiarity Falls, where a native village sits beside a station on Brazil's telegraph line.

events.detail: Expedition stays at the village and telegraph post at Utiarity Falls

headline: A live armadillo for the collection
summary: The rain stops though clouds hang on. Roosevelt heads out alone with his rifle and comes back carrying a living armadillo for naturalist Leo Miller, then sits by the falls watching the village men dance.

events.detail: Goes out with his rifle and returns with a live armadillo for Miller
Watches a dance by the village men beside the waterfall

headline: The expedition splits and heads north
summary: Father Zahm turns back for Tapirapoan with specimens, while Fiala and Lauriado break off to descend the Juruena. Under clearing skies, Roosevelt, Kermit, Rondon, Lyra, Olivera, Cherrie and Miller push on with mules and two ox carts, covering about 15 miles of wilderness.

events.detail: Father Zahm leaves for Tapirapoan carrying collected specimens
Fiala and Lauriado set off down the Juruena on a side expedition
Main party marches about 15 miles through the sertão with mule train and ox carts

uncertain: Lauriado's full name is not given; Fiala identified as Anthony Fiala.

headline: Biting insects at the Burity River
summary: Fair skies, fierce insects. The party camps on the western bank of the Burity, where the men wash in the river before rain moves in.

events.detail: March ends with camp on the west bank of the Burity River
A swim in the river, then rain

headline: Watching the Nhambiquara
summary: Through a downpour the party fords the Burity and camps where the Huatsui River begins, an automobile still traveling with them. Roosevelt studies the Nhambiquara people he meets along the way.

events.detail: Crosses the river in heavy rain and camps at the Huatsui headwaters
Observes the Nhambiquara people

headline: Lightening the load
summary: The expedition trims its baggage to travel lighter.

events.detail: Party reduces the amount of baggage it carries

headline: Camp on a Tapajós headwater
summary: A brief day's march ends at a stream that feeds the Tapajós. George Cherrie returns to camp with bird specimens.

events.detail: Short march; camp beside a headwater stream of the Tapajós
Cherrie collects birds

headline: Twenty miles to Juruena
summary: Under clear skies the party covers 20 miles and pulls into Juruena by mid-afternoon, an outpost with a garrison and a telegraph office.

events.detail: Reaches Juruena, a soldiers' post with a telegraph, after a 20-mile day

headline: A working rest day at Juruena
summary: The expedition stays put. Specimens are added to the collection, film is developed and journals caught up. Roosevelt watches native dancing as heavy rain falls.

events.detail: Party adds to the natural history collection
Photographs are developed
Notes and writing brought up to date
Roosevelt watches dances by local people

headline: Gibbon and Arsène Lupin by the campfire
summary: Back on the trail in the rain, the soaked party covers 15 miles and crosses the river by ferry. Evenings bring more campfire stories, and Roosevelt reads Gibbon alongside an Arsène Lupin detective tale.

events.detail: Leaves Juruena, marches 15 miles in rain and ferries across the river
Reads Gibbon and an Arsène Lupin story

headline: Marching on
summary: The expedition continues its overland march; no details are recorded.

events.detail: Expedition on the march

headline: Alice turns 30 back home
summary: Roosevelt's party is still marching through the interior. In the United States, his daughter Alice celebrates her 30th birthday.

events.detail: Expedition continues overland
Alice's 30th birthday in the United States

headline: Still on the trail
summary: The party keeps traveling; nothing more is recorded.

events.detail: Expedition travels on

headline: Another day of travel
summary: The expedition continues north with no further details noted.

events.detail: Expedition travels on

headline: Last of the carts at Campos Novos
summary: The party reaches Campos Novos and links up with Amilcar and Mello and the pack train. From here on, everything moves without carts.

Meets up with the pack train led by Amilcar and Mello
Carts are left behind for the rest of the journey

headline: An afternoon camp
summary: The expedition keeps moving and pitches camp in the afternoon.

events.detail: March; camp made in the afternoon

headline: Vilhena telegraph post
summary: The party arrives at the telegraph station of Vilhena. Back in the United States, Alice and Nick Longworth mark eight years of marriage.

events.detail: Reaches the telegraph station at Vilhena
Alice and Nicholas Longworth's 8th wedding anniversary

uncertain: The record misspells the station; the modern spelling Vilhena is used.

headline: Heading north
summary: The expedition continues northward.

events.detail: Party travels north

headline: Northward again
summary: Another day of northward travel, with nothing else recorded.

events.detail: Party travels north

headline: First sight of the River of Doubt
summary: After woods give way to open country, the party spots a small brook and recognizes it as the source of the Rio da Dúvida, the River of Doubt. Roosevelt jots notes on local people and their dances; rain falls.

Identifies a brook as the headwaters of the River of Doubt

headline: Attempted theft at camp
summary: Local people try to make off with things from the expedition's camp.

events.detail: Native people attempt to steal from camp

headline: Through hill pastures to Tres Burity
summary: The march crosses rolling grassland and reaches a ranch at Tres Burity.

events.detail: Marches over hilly pasture to the ranch at Tres Burity

headline: An archery exhibition at Bonifacio
summary: At Bonifacio, local Indians show off their skill with bows and arrows for the visitors.

events.detail: Indians stage an archery display

uncertain: The record has "Bonafacio"; this is likely the Jose Bonifacio post.

headline: Two parties, two rivers
summary: After seven miles the travelers meet Amilcar again and divide. Amilcar, Miller and Mello will follow the Gy-Paraná; Roosevelt, Kermit, Rondon, Lyra, Cherrie and the doctor take the River of Doubt with 16 paddlers, seven canoes and food for 50 days.

events.detail: Marches seven miles and rejoins Amilcar
Expedition divides between the Gy-Paraná and the River of Doubt

uncertain: The two-column roster is jumbled in the record, so it is unclear which group Olivera and Cajazeira joined.

headline: Fixing the camp's position
summary: The party's camp is plotted at about 12° south latitude, 60° west longitude. Roosevelt writes Robert Bridges about a chapter of his expedition book.

events.detail: Camp position recorded at roughly 12°1' S, 60°15' W
Writes Robert Bridges about a chapter of his Brazil book

letters.topic: A chapter of the book that became Through the Brazilian Wilderness

headline: Seven dugouts ready
summary: In camp, the expedition's seven canoes are all heavy dugouts hollowed from logs.

events.detail: All seven canoes are dugouts

headline: Into the unknown on the River of Doubt
summary: Roosevelt's party pushes off down the River of Doubt, a waterway no mapmaker has charted. They survey and measure the river as they paddle.

events.detail: Launches down the uncharted River of Doubt
Begins measuring and mapping the river

headline: Mapping the first stretch
summary: The survey canoes lead off while Cherrie gathers specimens near camp. Roosevelt and Cherrie follow around midday. Where the Bandeira joins, the river broadens; the team maps 16.5 kilometers. Film footage shows Roosevelt and the party in their canoes.

events.detail: Cherrie collects specimens around camp
Roosevelt and Cherrie embark about noon
River widens at the Bandeira confluence; 16.5 km mapped
Footage of Roosevelt and party in canoes

uncertain: The film note is hard to read in the record; it is treated as film footage of TR and the party on the river.

headline: Ants, bees and monkey for supper
summary: The men wash in the river before dawn, then paddle through heavy rain to map 20.5 kilometers. Stingless bees pester them, ants chew through even their clothing, and a monkey becomes dinner. In New York, Edith takes a hotel room to be near Ethel as her baby's birth approaches.

events.detail: Party maps 20.5 km of river in heavy rain
A monkey is shot and eaten
Edith moves into a New York hotel to await Ethel's delivery

headline: Scouting the Navaite rapids
summary: After 20 kilometers under light rain, the party camps and scouts the rapids ahead, which they name Navaite. Here the river squeezes to under 24 feet across.

events.detail: Travels 20 km and makes camp
Scouts and names the Navaite rapids where the river narrows below 24 feet

headline: Hauling dugouts around Navaite
summary: The whole day goes into dragging the heavy canoes and supplies overland past the rapids.

events.detail: Portages canoes and cargo around the rapids

headline: Fly dope and hungry termites
summary: The portage continues through pouring rain. The insects are so savage the men smear on 'fly dope,' and termites are devouring clothes and equipment.

events.detail: Portage continues in heavy rain
Insect repellent used; termites damage clothing and gear

headline: A sunken canoe raised
summary: The portage wraps up by morning. One dugout goes under and must be hauled back up before the party heads downriver again, faces and hands puffy from bites. They make 12 kilometers and camp among giant ants.

events.detail: Completes the portage
A sunken canoe is raised
Paddles 12 km and camps; giant ants observed

headline: Winding river, slow progress
summary: The twisting river yields 19 kilometers. The men gather wild honey and sample the sap of the 'milk-tree.' Rapids ahead mean another portage. After 100 river kilometers, they sit just 55 kilometers, as the crow flies, from the starting point.

events.detail: Covers 19 km on a winding stretch
Men collect honey and try milk-tree sap
Rapids ahead are scouted; another portage needed

headline: A grandson born in New York
summary: On the river, the party moves camp around the rapids while Kermit finds yet another rapid downstream. In New York City, Ethel delivers an eight-pound boy after a 48-hour labor: Richard Derby Jr., Roosevelt's grandson.

events.detail: Portage and camp shift
Kermit scouts ahead and finds another rapid
Ethel gives birth to Richard Derby Jr.

headline: French poetry from Kermit
summary: While the portage goes on, Roosevelt hunts in the forest without luck. Kermit loans him a volume of French poems.

events.detail: Portage continues
Hunts in the woods but finds nothing
Borrows a book of French poetry from Kermit

headline: Portage day
summary: Another day spent carrying canoes and gear around the rapids.

events.detail: Portage

headline: Running two rapids
summary: The canoes travel just 1.5 kilometers but shoot two rapids rather than carrying around them. The pests never let up: ants, termites and biting flies.

events.detail: Advances 1.5 km, running two rapids
Constant trouble from ants, flies and termites

headline: Two canoes smashed overnight
summary: Two dugouts tear loose in the night and are wrecked in the current. The party will have to carve replacements.

events.detail: Two canoes break free overnight and are destroyed

headline: Carving a new dugout
summary: The men set to hollowing out a huge tree trunk for a canoe. Roosevelt hunts in the forest, while Kermit has better luck finding food elsewhere.

events.detail: Crew hollows out a tree for a new canoe
Roosevelt hunts in the woods
Kermit brings in food

headline: Working by candlelight
summary: Canoe building goes on from morning until ten at night, the last hours lit by candles.

events.detail: Canoe building runs until 10 p.m.

headline: Racing the rapids to save food
summary: In drenching rain the new canoe is launched near noon and the party moves again. Short on time and food, they run the rapids, bailing after each one, until past 5 p.m., making 16 km and camping in darkness. The Outlook prints his 'South America and the Monroe Doctrine.'

events.detail: New canoe launched around midday
Runs rapids into the evening, 16 km, camp pitched after dark
'South America and the Monroe Doctrine' appears in The Outlook

works.title: South America and the Monroe Doctrine

headline: Simplicio drowns; Kermit nearly lost
summary: After 6 easy kilometers the party hears rapids. Scouting them, Kermit's canoe is caught by a whirlpool and swept over. Paddler Simplicio is killed; Kermit, pulled under, fights his way out, and his dog reaches shore too. Simplicio is buried before camp.

events.detail: Drifts 6 km before reaching rapids
Kermit's canoe capsizes in a whirlpool; Simplicio drowns
Kermit narrowly escapes drowning
Simplicio is buried

headline: Losing the rope and pulleys
summary: Under black skies and blinding rain, loads go overland and empty canoes run the rapids. One lost canoe carried the ropes and pulleys, ending heavy portages. Indians kill Kermit's dog. With four canoes and two-thirds of the food left, men will walk the banks, spare clothes are dropped, and quinine is given daily.

events.detail: Cargo carried overland while canoes run the rapids
Canoe carrying rope and pulleys is lost
Kermit's dog is killed by Indians
Loads and clothing reduced; 13 men to walk the bank
Doctor gives quinine daily; barefoot men suffer bites

uncertain: The record says only "the dog"; context points to Kermit's dog.

headline: Half walking, half paddling
summary: Rondon, Lyra, Kermit, Cherrie and nine others hike the bank, while Roosevelt, the doctor and six men, three of them lamed by swollen feet, ride the canoes. They cover 7 kilometers and run two rapids.

events.detail: Shore party walks the bank
Roosevelt rides in the canoes with the doctor and invalids; 7 km and two rapids

headline: The Rio Roosevelt gets its name
summary: A tributary is found joining the river and named Rio Kermit, while the main stream itself gets a new name: Rio Roosevelt. The canoes shoot another set of rapids and slip past an Indian village, covering 8 km.

events.detail: Tributary named Rio Kermit; River of Doubt renamed Rio Roosevelt
Runs rapids and passes an Indian village; 8 km

headline: Swimming with piranha
summary: The men build more canoes. Some go swimming despite piranha in the water, and ants overrun the camp.

events.detail: Work begins on new canoes
Men swim though piranha are present; ants swarm camp

headline: Exploring the forest
summary: As canoe building continues, Roosevelt explores the surrounding forest.

events.detail: Canoe building
Roosevelt explores the forest

headline: Chile essay appears at home
summary: The crew keeps working on canoes. In The Outlook, Roosevelt's 'Chile and the Monroe Doctrine' is published.

events.detail: Canoe building
'Chile and the Monroe Doctrine' published in The Outlook

headline: Six canoes and moving again
summary: With two fresh dugouts, the fleet stands at six. The party gets underway and covers 10 km, though easing the canoes down the newest rapids eats up six hours.

events.detail: Two new canoes completed
Travels 10 km; six hours spent at rapids

headline: Cherrie talks of Vermont
summary: The party makes 13 km, seven hours of it working through a 4-km stretch of rapids. Cherrie talks about his home in Vermont.

events.detail: 13 km, including a long rapid
Cherrie talks about home in Vermont

headline: Eating palm hearts
summary: With rations shrinking, the men cut palm tops to eat. Big rapids hold progress to 1.5 km.

events.detail: Palm tops harvested for food as supplies run low
Only 1.5 km made through heavy rapids

headline: Half the food gone
summary: After bringing the canoes through the rapids, the party names a tributary the Taunay. Half the provisions are eaten, two men have fever, and more rapids rumble ahead. At home, Edith returns from New York and opens Sagamore Hill.

events.detail: Canoes brought down rapids
Tributary named the Taunay River
Two men sick with fever
Edith returns to Sagamore Hill

uncertain: The note 'Opened the house' is from the Sagamore Hill record, not TR, and is not quoted.

headline: Rock carvings found
summary: The three most skilled boatmen take the canoes through the rapids. The party discovers carved symbols on rocks.

events.detail: Best boatmen run the canoes down the rapids
Petroglyphs discovered

headline: Drenched and worn out
summary: Three kilometers bring more rapids, which take the whole day. After a ten-minute paddle, still more rapids appear. In heavy rain, the men camp soaked and exhausted.

events.detail: Short runs broken by rapids; camp in heavy rain

headline: A cataract ahead
summary: The canoes shoot rapids and pass a stream the party names the Cherrie River. Kermit finds a perilous three-kilometer cataract downstream, so the loads must be cut further.

events.detail: Runs rapids
Names the Cherrie River
Kermit discovers a dangerous cataract ahead
Canoe loads reduced again

headline: Lowering canoes through a gorge
summary: The men ease the canoes down rapids inside a steep-sided gorge.

events.detail: Canoes lowered by hand down rapids in a gorge

headline: Packing loads over a mountain
summary: Canoe lowering continues while the cargo is carried up and over the mountain.

events.detail: Canoes lowered; loads hauled over the mountain

headline: One monkey for the whole party
summary: A single monkey is shot, giving each man a few good bites. In heavy rain five canoes come down safely and a sixth breaks. Insects eat Roosevelt's last clothes. At home, Scribners publishes his two-volume natural history of African big game, written with Edmund Heller.

events.detail: Five canoes lowered safely; one broken
One monkey shot and shared
Insects destroy Roosevelt's clothing

works.title: Life Histories of African Game Animals
A Hunter-Naturalist in the Brazilian Wilderness

uncertain: The record is cut off where it names where A Hunter-Naturalist in the Brazilian Wilderness appeared.

headline: Spirits sag among the men
summary: The canoes are finally all lowered, but some of the men are losing heart.

events.detail: Finishes lowering the canoes
Morale falls among some of the men

headline: Three kilometers and another gorge
summary: Underway again, the party manages only 3 km, most of the men on foot. Ahead lie more rapids in a deep canyon.

events.detail: Advances 3 km with most men walking

headline: Murder in camp
summary: Starting down the rapids, the party loses a canoe; the boots and clothing of Kermit and Lyra are falling apart. Then Julio, one of the paddlers, shoots and kills fellow camarada Paishon. Edith writes Bamie with news.

events.detail: Descent of rapids begins; a canoe lost
Kermit's and Lyra's clothing and boots are rotting
Paddler Julio shoots and kills Paishon
Edith writes Bamie with news

headline: Roosevelt's leg strikes a boulder
summary: While working a canoe through the rapids, Roosevelt slams his leg against a rock and comes down with fever. Kermit has dysentery. At home, Ethel marks her first wedding anniversary.

events.detail: Descent of rapids continues
Kermit sick with dysentery
Roosevelt injures his leg on a boulder
Roosevelt develops fever
Ethel's first wedding anniversary

headline: Delirious with fever
summary: Julio is spotted in the jungle but left alone and never seen again. Roosevelt's fever climbs to 39°C; out of his head, he recites poetry as the party keeps working down the rapids.

events.detail: Descent of rapids continues
Julio sighted in the forest and left behind
Roosevelt delirious with a 39°C fever, reciting poetry

headline: Roosevelt asks to be left behind
summary: As the party portages more rapids, Roosevelt urges his companions to go on without him so they can survive. Far away in Bogota, American and Colombian envoys sign a treaty, negotiated under Secretary of State Bryan, that voices regret over the 1903 loss of Panama and promises Colombia $25 million.

events.detail: Portages rapids
Roosevelt begs the party to abandon him

headline: Thirty-six kilometers of flat water
summary: The land flattens and the party makes 36 km, passing a large unmapped river that joins the Rio Roosevelt.

events.detail: Covers 36 km over flat country
Passes a large unknown tributary

headline: Monkeys and piranha for food
summary: Only 5 km today through a chain of rapids; cargo goes around two of them before the canoes are run. Three monkeys and two piranha go into the pot.

events.detail: 5 km through rapids, carrying loads past two
Party shoots three monkeys and catches two piranha

headline: Archie turns 20
summary: The expedition is in camp. At Harvard, Archie celebrates his 20th birthday.

events.detail: Party in camp
Archie's 20th birthday

headline: Wishing for a birch-bark canoe
summary: Run, portage, run, more rapids: under 5 km in all. Roosevelt wishes for a light birch-bark canoe instead of the cumbersome dugouts. A toucan, piranha and a turtle feed the party.

events.detail: Short runs and portages; under 5 km
Toucan, piranha and turtle taken for food

uncertain: The record points to Oscar King Davis's Released for Publication for TR's thoughts of suicide on the expedition; this is not stated as an event of this day.

headline: Still burning with fever
summary: Loads are carried down to the base of the rapids, followed by a 30- to 40-minute run before more rapids appear. Roosevelt remains feverish. At Sagamore Hill, Clifford and Teresa Richardson are guests.

events.detail: Loads portaged; short run before more rapids
Roosevelt still has fever
Clifford and Teresa Richardson recorded as guests

uncertain: Guest-book entry assumed to be at Sagamore Hill, with TR absent.

headline: An Easter feast of fish
summary: On Easter Sunday the party paddles ten minutes and portages for eight hours, but 28 big fish mean everyone eats well for once.

events.detail: Easter Sunday
Ten-minute run, eight-hour portage
Catches 28 large fish; the whole party eats its fill

headline: Silence at last
summary: After a day of portaging, a late 15-km run brings the party to a camp where, the roar of rapids is gone for the first time in more than a month.

events.detail: Portage, then a 15-km run late in the day
No sound of rapids at camp for the first time in weeks

headline: Sickened by nuts and meat
summary: A 32-km run takes the canoes through a few minor rapids and one portage. The men fall ill after eating nuts and meat.

events.detail: 32 km; light rapids run, one portage
Men sickened by nuts and meat

headline: Out of the wilderness
summary: Still queasy, the men cover 25 km and spot 'J.A.' carved on a post, a rubber tapper's mark. Houses follow, then talk with settlers: they have made it out. Roosevelt's fever lingers; abscesses on his leg need a drain, and Rondon notes erysipelas in the left leg hurt in 1902.

events.detail: Covers 25 km
Finds a rubber tapper's carved initials and reaches settlements
Roosevelt's leg abscess drained; Rondon notes erysipelas

headline: Downriver from house to house
summary: The party makes long runs downstream each day, spending nights at riverside homes.

events.detail: Long day's travel downriver; overnight at a house

headline: No more foraging
summary: Roosevelt purchases provisions for the men, ending their need to live off the land.

events.detail: Travel continues
Roosevelt buys food for the crew

headline: Still sick on the river
summary: The trip downstream goes on with Roosevelt still ill.

events.detail: Travel continues
Roosevelt remains sick

headline: A guide and a gift from Senhor Barboso
summary: The party engages a rubber worker as guide. Senhor Barboso supplies a canoe and food and will not take payment. Past the mouth of the Rio Branco, they portage rapids; the cook buys a trumpeter bird.

events.detail: Hires a rubber man as guide

A trumpeter bird is bought

headline: A shelter for the invalid
summary: A sun shelter is rigged over the ailing Roosevelt in the lighter canoe they acquired. A stop at a store yields sugar and tobacco, and the party covers 52 km. In Colorado, National Guard troops massacre striking miners at Ludlow.

events.detail: Shelter built in the canoe for Roosevelt; 52 km
Buys sugar and tobacco at a store
Ludlow Massacre of striking miners in Colorado

headline: Trading dugouts for boats
summary: A good day's run brings the party to the Inferno rapids. At a house they pick up a large boat and a light one, leaving two dugouts behind.

events.detail: Runs to the Inferno rapids
Obtains two boats and leaves two dugouts

headline: Down the Inferno rapids
summary: Canoes, boats and gear are worked down the Inferno rapids, a brief run, in the rain.

events.detail: Descends the Inferno rapids

headline: Nearly 50 kilometers
summary: The canoes cover close to 50 km and shoot the Infernino rapids fully loaded. Night is spent in a grimy house.

events.detail: About 50 km; runs the Infernino rapids loaded
Overnight in a dirty house

headline: Last dugout replaced
summary: Fifty kilometers bring the party to the Carupanan rapids. At a store run by Senhor Caripe, they receive a boat to replace their final dugout.

events.detail: 50 km to the Carupanan rapids
Senhor Caripe provides a boat in place of the last dugout

headline: Kermit shoots a caiman

events.detail: Descends Carupanan rapids with Caripe as guide
Kermit shoots a caiman

headline: Flags at the Castanho
summary: Past the last dangerous rapids, at 1 p.m. the party reaches the Castanho, where Lieutenant Pyrineus has waited a month, Brazilian and American flags flying. Where the two rivers meet, they form the Aripuanã.

headline: The Rio Roosevelt made official
summary: In a small ceremony Rondon lays out the expedition's findings and formally names the river Rio Roosevelt: 750 km in two months by canoe. Leaving Lyra and Pyrineus, the boats reach São João at 1 p.m. in heavy rain, and Roosevelt lodges with Senhor Caripe.

headline: Steamer to Manaus
summary: At São João the party abandons boat and canoe and boards Pyrineus's river steamer for a 36-hour trip to Manaus.

events.detail: Boards Pyrineus's river steamer for Manaus

headline: Into the Amazon
summary: The steamer works down the lower Madeira and enters the Amazon in the afternoon. Back home, Corinne marks her 32nd wedding anniversary.

Corinne's 32nd wedding anniversary

headline: Reaching Manaus

headline: Leaving Manaus

summary: Aboard ship on the Amazon, Roosevelt tells his English friend Arthur Lee about his fever and abscesses and looks ahead to a visit to England.

headline: A quiet, thin homecoming
summary: Roosevelt lands in New York 35 pounds lighter, on a cane, helped by two men, and jokes about his 'big stick.' His wife Edith and sons Ted and Archie are waiting; there are no crowds or parades. Edith and Dr. Lambert have the yacht Joyance carry him to Oyster Bay.

Met by Edith, Ted and Archie
Taken to Oyster Bay aboard the yacht Joyance

headline: Politics resumes at Sagamore Hill
summary: Home one day, Roosevelt meets with Perkins and Pinchot; Frances Kellor, Lillian Wald and Dr. Lambert call. He writes Ruth and Arthur Lee about his exploring, the skeptics, and his new grandson.

headline: Oyster Bay welcomes him home
summary: Roosevelt sees Robert Bacon at The Outlook, and Oyster Bay holds an official homecoming. He writes General Francis V. Greene that he would raise a cavalry regiment if war with Mexico came.

headline: A full house of Progressives
summary: Roosevelt meets with William Flinn, Pinchot, Wilkinson, Perkins, Oscar King Davis, Robert Bass and Knox. Stoddard, Mark Sullivan and Edmund Heller call. He writes Dan Hanna about the elections and Progressivism and thanks Charles Fairbanks.

headline: Brazil lecture in Washington
